item.title: Why Do Our Moral Views Keep Changing?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Why Do Our Moral Views Keep Changing?

Research suggests moral change is a sign of seeing new reasons.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Most people treat their own moral views as unchangeable, and believe those who disagree with them are wrong.
  • People actually develop new moral views, form new connections, and change their views on competing concerns.
  • Understanding why morals change doesn't determine if those changes are good or bad.
Source: Olga/Adobe Stock

Most of us hold a handful of moral truths we consider unmovable. For example, violence, lying, and slavery are wrong. Yet, people regularly act against these truths. Some people cheer for violence in war or sports, others lie multiple times a day, and for centuries, otherwise reasonable people defended slavery.

The gap between what we believe and how we behave raises an uncomfortable question: Are our moral principles easily overridden by selfishness or circumstances?

Audun Dahl’s Theory on Shifting Moral Views

Not necessarily, according to a new book by Audun Dahl, associate professor of psychology at Cornell's College of Human Ecology and director of the Developmental Moral Psychology Lab. His book, Between Fixed and Fickle: Why Our Moral Views Keep Changing, draws on decades of research to offer an evidence-based theory of why moral views shift.

Dahl describes a familiar pattern of thinking he calls the story of the "fixed and fickle." First, we treat our own moral convictions as fixed and self-evident — so obvious that no reasonable, well-meaning person could see things differently. But when we encounter people who disagree, we conclude their moral sense must be fickle — easily corrupted by self-interest, irrationality, or unruly emotion.

It's a tidy explanation, and a flattering one as it lets us keep our convictions intact while writing off anyone who disagrees with us. It's also politically useful, since it insulates one's followers against the other side's counterarguments.

“In that story, moral change gets chalked up to amoral forces, across the lifespan, across situations and across history,” Dahl said. “My book tries to rid us of that story, outside and inside psychology.”

Dahl’s book points out a blind spot in the “fixed and fickle” explanation: it's usually a story we tell about other people. Few of us look back at our own moral evolution from childhood through adulthood and attribute changes to our own selfishness or poor reasoning. We tend to assume we got lucky and ended up with the "correct" morality, while everyone who disagrees must have gone wrong somewhere.

Dahl's Three Reasons for Moral Change

Dahl's alternative explanation is that people typically change their moral views when they encounter genuine reasons to do so. His book identifies three types of reasons that people change their beliefs.

  1. People can develop new moral concerns, such as believing that all current and future humans deserve equal rights.
  2. They can form new connections between existing concerns and new issues. For example, someone may realize that today's fossil fuel use will harm tomorrow's children.
  3. People can shift how they balance competing concerns. For instance, they can decide that modest sacrifices today, like flying less, or eating less meat, are worth it to slow climate change and protect future generations.

“These three types of reasons for moral change can bring changes across our lifetimes, from one situation to the next, or even across history,” Dahl said.

In the book, Dahl makes an important point: Understanding why someone changes their moral views is separate from evaluating whether that change was positive or negative.

“Science can help us realize why our moral views keep changing, but it can’t tell us how our moral views ought to change,” he said. “When you learn the reasons for my moral changes, you might judge me more mildly, or you might judge me more harshly, depending on what you learned my reasons are.”

The take-home message is: The next time you find yourself baffled by someone whose moral views differ sharply from your own, or surprised by how much your own views have shifted over time, it's worth thinking about the reasons behind the change. Dahl's research suggests that kind of curiosity tends to reveal a much less cynical picture of human nature than the "fixed and fickle" story would have us believe.

item.title: A Bride's Guide to Managing Panic
item.description:
Anxiety

A Bride's Guide to Managing Panic

Don't let panic steal your wedding memories.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Panic attacks affect millions of people, making wedding-day anxiety common.
  • Exposure therapy exercises can help reduce panic before one's wedding day.
  • Mindful breathing and grounding through the senses can calm panic symptoms during the wedding ceremony.

Supporting a bride with panic attacks was the first time my clinical career intersected with my wedding coordinator experience. It was a genesis moment for something that has become a specialty. The bride had panic attacks and was particularly concerned with walking down the aisle. There was a chance that the wedding was not going to happen.

This may seem very specific, but according to the ADAA, panic disorder affects about 6 million people in the United States. Anxiety disorders that may include having panic attacks impact about 40 million people each year (National Alliance on Mental Illness). This is about 19 percent of the population. With numbers this high, it is also likely that many people managing panic attacks are also getting married in the next year.

You do not need to let a fear of panic attacks steal your wedding day. If you have been considering downsizing or even canceling a wedding that you actually want to have, keep reading. As a disclaimer: My focus is on women because they are often a focal point in ceremonies and are more likely than men to suffer from panic disorder.

What is a panic attack?

For those who may be unsure, a panic attack is a sudden intense rush of fear and anxiety accompanied by several other cognitive and physiological symptoms. This can include racing thoughts, hyperventilating, trembling, and difficulty breathing, but this list is more extensive than that.

Panic attacks are much more than just anxiety. The sudden onset is extremely disruptive, and the symptoms are often visible to others. They occasionally lead people to seek medical attention at emergency rooms, but most often, they cause avoidance.

How to treat panic before your wedding day

Luckily, there are some incredibly effective behavioral treatments for panic. If you have a little time (three to four months), I recommend finding a cognitive-behavioral therapist. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), you will learn ways to challenge anxiety-based thoughts and skills to manage physiological symptoms. The therapist can lead you through specific skills and exercises to retrain both the brain and body’s reactions.

Exposure therapy is truly going to be key, and there are two main types you will want to make sure the therapist can guide you through. Interoceptive exposure will help bring on the symptoms of a panic attack (in a controlled way). Experiencing the symptoms in a safe environment will effectively help reduce their impact. It helps you become more familiar with the sensations, ultimately reducing fear of them. It takes the surprise away from the symptoms, helping you create new associations.

In vivo exposure brings you out of the therapy room and into the world. If it is possible to arrange, you may practice walking down the aisle or just being in the ceremony space. Ask the venue if you can spend time there, or maybe find a similar space. Some therapists, but not all, may be able to go with you. This is how I helped the bride I mentioned. I, along with a small team of others, created a mock wedding. We practiced the ceremony until it felt comfortable. Exposure therapy like this is a little harder to coordinate, but not impossible. Even if that sort of practice is unavailable, any CBT therapist can help you construct a specific exposure experience to do between sessions and evaluate it with you afterwards.

How to reduce panic during the wedding ceremony

During the ceremony, I recommend grounding through your senses. The point is to focus on something external to you and let internal sensations fade into the background. You do not want to be scanning your body for potential panic symptoms instead of enjoying your wedding. To use sight, find a focal point. (I would suggest your partner, at the end of the aisle or standing next to you during vows.) To use your sense of smell, choose a particularly fragrant flower in your bouquet and focus on that. At the end of the ceremony, ground through your sense of touch. Hold hands; squeeze tightly if you need to.

Another option is being mindful of breathing. You have probably heard this before, so let me share more about why this strategy can work. It is best to focus on larger, slow breaths, but when we get anxious, we take shorter, shallow breaths automatically. When you are mindful of your breath, you have influence over it. Shallow breathing can actually tell our body that we need to prepare for something bad to happen. We get tense, hyperaware of our body, and we sweat. This further activates our fight-or-flight response and can cause panic attacks. But when you take a deep breath, you expand your chest, which reduces muscle tension and opens your posture. Doing this sends a message from your body to your brain that there is nothing to worry about.

These last two strategies are meant to activate mindfulness (present-focused, non-judgmental awareness). This is on purpose. Mindfulness is meant to help you be in the moment, and hopefully create lasting happy memories of your wedding. Whether you have a lot or a little time, hopefully this guide can help support your wedding goals.

item.title: Just Say No to Alcohol?
item.description:
Alcoholism

Just Say No to Alcohol?

Consuming 14 drinks weekly may carry a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of alcohol death.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • A major new study finds no net health benefit from low-level alcohol use.
  • If you drink, less is better; if you don’t drink, there’s no medical reason to start.
  • Cancer is increasingly recognized as alcohol's most important public health consequence.

A major new study from Sinead George of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health finds no net health benefit from low-level alcohol consumption and estimates a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of alcohol-attributable death among people consuming 14 drinks per week. The once-popular view that moderate drinking is healthy is increasingly challenged by current evidence, which indicates that risks such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, and injury may outweigh any potential benefits.

When I posted Just Say No to Alcohol? in 2024, I argued that the science was moving away from the old French wine paradox, that moderate drinking was good for us. The long-standing image of a nightly glass of wine as health-promoting was already beginning to crack back then. Then George et al. found no significant net health benefit from low-level drinking. Zero, nada, zilch.

George and colleagues estimated the lifetime risk of alcohol-attributable mortality and morbidity in the United States based on a person's average lifetime alcohol consumption, also examining the impact of drinking patterns on health.

No French Wine Paradox
Source: Dr Mark Gold /Used with permission

The Alcohol Intake and Health study arrived amid mounting evidence that alcohol contributes to cancer, cardiac arrhythmias, liver disease, injuries, and addiction—even among people who do not have alcohol use disorder. Alcohol remains one of the leading preventable causes of death in the United States, responsible for more than 170,000 deaths annually and millions of years of potential life lost.

Rather than asking whether drinkers live longer than nondrinkers, the Alcohol Intake and Health Study investigators estimated the lifetime risk of diseases and injuries caused by alcohol itself.

Their conclusion deserves attention from addiction specialists and the general public. Drinking 14 drinks per week—formerly the upper limit of U.S. guidance for men—was associated with roughly a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of an alcohol-attributable death.

Women generally experience greater alcohol-related health risks than men at the same level of consumption. Compared with men, women achieve higher blood alcohol concentrations from equivalent alcohol intake because of differences in body composition and first-pass alcohol metabolism. As a result, women develop alcohol-related liver disease, cardiomyopathy, neurotoxicity, and several alcohol-associated cancers at lower cumulative levels of exposure and shorter durations of drinking. Maybe some women can “drink a man under the table.” But at what health cost to the woman?

Why This Study Matters

For decades, alcohol's reputation as healthy was supported by studies suggesting that moderate drinkers appeared healthier than abstainers. Many of those studies were limited by methodological shortcomings, including the inclusion of former drinkers in the abstainer group and inadequate adjustment for socioeconomic, behavioral, and other lifestyle differences. In the new analysis, researchers modeled diseases and injuries with established causal links to alcohol consumption, including multiple cancers, liver disease, cardiovascular disease, infectious diseases, and injuries.

There were small signals of possible cardiovascular benefits at very low consumption levels, consistent with earlier research. But when alcohol-related cancers, liver disease, infections, injuries, suicides, and other causes of death were included, those apparent benefits disappeared. This distinction is critical.

The question is no longer whether alcohol might slightly reduce the risk of one disease. The relevant question is whether drinking improves overall health when all consequences are considered together. According to this study, it does not.

Cancer Risks

For many people, alcohol still evokes images of cirrhosis, alcoholism, and drunk driving. Modern alcohol research increasingly points elsewhere: cancer. Alcohol is categorized as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, meaning there is conclusive evidence that it causes cancer in humans. Breast cancer, colorectal cancer, esophageal cancer, oral cancers, liver cancer, and several other malignancies become more common as alcohol consumption rises. Important, the risks are not limited to heavy drinkers.

One reason the public has been slow to absorb this message is that cancer develops slowly and quietly. There is no hangover from alcohol-induced DNA damage. There is no obvious warning sign when alcohol alters hormonal pathways or promotes carcinogenesis. A person can feel perfectly healthy while unknowingly increasing their long-term cancer risk through drinking. This reality has become difficult to ignore.

The study estimated that lifetime alcohol-attributable mortality exceeded 1 in 1,000 at approximately one drink per day and exceeded 1 in 100 at roughly eight to nine drinks per week. At 14 drinks weekly, the estimated risk of dying from an alcohol-caused condition reached approximately 4 percent, or 1 in 25.

Public health officials routinely use lifetime risk thresholds when evaluating environmental toxins, occupational exposures, and other hazards. If another consumer product carried a lifetime mortality risk of 1 in 25, public concern would likely be substantial. Among adults younger than 40, the study found, there is no net protective effect from alcohol. In younger populations, alcohol-related mortality is driven largely by injuries, motor vehicle crashes, violence, and self-harm rather than cardiovascular disease. The risks are immediate. Any possible cardiovascular benefits remain distant, uncertain, and largely irrelevant to younger adults.

One other lesson repeatedly emerging from alcohol research is that average consumption tells only part of the story. Seven drinks spread across seven days are not equivalent to seven drinks consumed on a Saturday night.

The study reviewed evidence showing that binge drinking can eliminate any apparent cardiovascular advantages associated with moderate average consumption. Heavy episodic drinking was associated with sharply increased risks of cardiovascular events, injury, suicide attempts, and motor vehicle crashes.

Before Alcohol Use Disorder Develops

As an addiction physician, I am especially interested in what the data mean in support of intervention before alcohol use disorder develops.

One theme I have discussed repeatedly in this blog is that we should stop waiting for people to "hit bottom" before recommending treatment. We screen for hypertension before stroke occurs. We identify prediabetes before blindness or kidney failure develops. We act early because prevention works. Alcohol should be no different.

The harms associated with alcohol are not confined to people with severe alcohol use disorder. Many harms occur among individuals who consider themselves normal drinkers. Cancer risk, injury risk, and cardiovascular complications do not require a diagnosis of alcoholism.

The traditional distinction between "problem drinkers" and everyone else is becoming increasingly difficult to defend scientifically.

The Bottom Line

Perhaps the most important implication of this study is that there is no credible medical justification for advising a nondrinker to begin drinking for health reasons. That idea sounds strange today, but physicians once offered exactly that advice.

The Alcohol Intake and Health Study does not prove that everyone who drinks should immediately stop. Nor does it suggest someone who occasionally enjoys a glass of wine is destined for illness.

What it does show is that the old narrative—that moderate drinking is good for health—has become increasingly difficult to defend.

Large international analyses have reached similar conclusions. When cancer and injury are considered alongside cardiovascular outcomes, the level of alcohol consumption associated with the lowest overall health risk appears very close to zero.

The most accurate message may be surprisingly simple: If you do not drink, there is no medical reason to start. If you do drink, less is generally better. And if your goal is maximizing health and longevity, the evidence increasingly points in the same direction: Alcohol offers considerably more risk than benefit.

item.title: The Beatles Shared Credit on Every Song. I Didn't
item.description:
Relationships

The Beatles Shared Credit on Every Song. I Didn't

Personal Perspective: Lennon and McCartney made a pact at 16. I broke mine.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Lennon and McCartney agreed at 16 to put both their names on every song they wrote
  • Boys are often socialized in hierarchy and competition. This limits their later intimacy in relationships.
  • Many couples unconsciously rank each other's value in a 95/70 dynamic.
  • You can be only as happy in a relationship as your least happy partner.
You're only as happy as your least happy partner.
Source: Miri Yogev

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

I fell in love with the Beatles as a kid. Starting with Twist and Shout, like every other kid. As a teenager, it was the Sgt. Pepper psychedelic, mysterious, trippy feel that drew me. And since then, I keep rediscovering them every couple of decades.

Now in my fourth decade, I am a couples therapist discovering them again. This time it is not because of their music but because of one decision they made before any of the music existed.

When John Lennon and Paul McCartney were teenagers, long before the fame and the screaming crowds, they made an agreement. Everything either of them wrote would carry both names. Not Lennon. Not McCartney. Both.

Lennon-McCartney

It didn't matter who wrote the verse or the bridge, the lyrics or the music. Both names went on it. They shook on this at 16, and they kept it.

Think about who these two men were. Two of the most talented songwriters who ever lived, each one able to write a complete song without the other. Each of them was whole. They chose to share the credit anyway.

That is rare. It is especially rare between two men.

Here is why. Most of us men grew up inside a hierarchy. Terry Real calls it psychological patriarchy, in which we separate the male from the female and position one above the other. You breathe it in. You internalize it. So we learn early to fight the other man. Because in a hierarchy, if I am not above you, I am below you. There is no third option. That is the price many men pay.

The training works. It works in the schoolyard, the workplace, the army. You climb. You win. Then you fall in love, and the same socialization turns into poison.

"Where there is hierarchy, there is no intimacy." Galit Romanelli

Every relationship starts in a hierarchy. We have written about how many couples unconsciously set up a 95/70 dynamic, one partner valued at 95 percent, the other at 70, quietly dividing up who gets to be better at what. The work of evolving, maturing, and "remarrying" your partner is the slow move out of that hierarchy and into relational equilibrium. Hierarchy turned on its side becomes a spectrum.

So when two 16-year-old boys, full of talent and ego, chose to flatten the hierarchy between them before the music even started, they did something almost no man does. They blocked their own exits. They made it impossible to keep score. That liberated them to focus on the music and not on their ego.

I have seen couples fight over credit a thousand times in the clinic. But today I am not going to talk about them. Today I am going to talk about me.

I know all of this because I did exactly that. When it was time to write my book Feel Free Together—How to Remarry Your Partner, I wrote it alone. The truth is that the whole model in that book came from my marriage. Thanks to Galit I knew viscerally how it feels to unbalance your marriage and remarry and not just preach to couples the theory and idea. It was a joint effort full of blood, sweat, and tears, that helped us crystalize the relational blueprint that we now teach couples. Sixteen years together, and every step we have taken toward relational equality has asked me to give up some of my perceived height.

Galit never asked to be the co-author of the book. She did not fight me for it. She let me have it, because she knew I needed it for my own ego, in my process of "recovering" from the hierarchical masculinity I grew up in.

I was aware of the 95/70 mentality the whole time I was writing. In the acknowledgments at the end of the book I wrote:

"... This book is yours as much as it is mine. Thank you for understanding that I needed to write it alone, for my ego. The truth is, it is really our book."

I wrote that. Then I continued to put my name on the cover.

I didn't do Lennon-McCartney.

The Beatles were not clean of this either. They fought later. The egos came back. The money and the lawyers came in, and by the end Lennon and McCartney could barely stand each other. But they had blocked their own exits. The names held. Sixty years later, every one of those songs still says Lennon-McCartney. The pact outlived the friendship. They felt the same pull I felt. They were just smarter, earlier.

Here's what I have learned. You can be only as happy as your least happy partner.

Her being your equal is not a gift you hand her.
Source: MIri Yogev

It ensures that you’ll be able to enjoy the relationship, without scorekeeping or competing.

Galit is finishing her Ph.D. right now. When she does, the degrees between us will be even. We are walking into a new era, and I can feel the old hierarchy creeping up on me. I am trying not to. I am slowly learning what Lennon and McCartney knew at 16 and hope to fully master before I'm 64.

So I will ask you what I am asking myself.

Where in your relationship are you collecting credit for something that belongs to both of you? Where are you the only name on the cover of something you couldn't make alone?

It does not have to be a book. It could be the parenting move you take credit for. The change you call your idea. The thing you brought home and forgot whose it really was.

So where are you not releasing your relational hierarchy?

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D.-candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: When World Cup Fans Transformed a City
item.description:
Awe

When World Cup Fans Transformed a City

Boston’s World Cup experience highlighted collective effervescence.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Collective effervescence is a healing experience of awe that restores one's sense of community and humanity.
  • Collective effervescence can be shared and enjoyed by watching World Cup games, especially in host cities.
  • Recognizing awe experiences through the Awe Experience Scale validates collective effervescence in action.
Source: Pexels, Andreus Simkus

Bummed by cold, rainy weekends or sweltering heat waves, by never-ending bad news and a loss of faith in humanity, most Bostonians, as most Americans, have been stuck in drab survival mode. People are more guarded and edgy; they don’t easily smile or casually chat. A recent poll from the Institute of Politics at Harvard Kennedy School reported that social trust has declined over the past five years.

But then came an amazing surprise: The Tartan Army of about 40,000-50,000 Scottish fans for the FIFA World Cup arrived in reveling droves—with bagpipes and wearing kilts. Bostonians hardly knew what hit them. How did these hilariously wild lads get away with putting traffic cones on our precious statues and drinking all our beer? Even the iconic statue of George Washington on his high horse got coned. “No Scotland, no party,” chanted the charming revelers—and the singing was contagious.

For Scotland's first World Cup appearance in 28 years, the Tartan Army stayed in Boston and Providence to watch the match against Haiti at Boston Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. On the day of the game on June 13th, the total stadium attendance of 64,000 was packed with a majority of Scottish fans who boldly sang their national anthem in unison—and the decibel level of 125 dB of their singing was the highest crowd noise ever recorded at a World Cup game.

And Scotland won.

On the days before this match and certainly after their victory, thousands of Scottish fans alongside fans of Iraq, Norway, Haiti, and Morocco filled the streets and bars of Boston and Providence, drawing locals into their jubilant antics and sharing the buzz, the whimsy, and friendliness. Bostonians got a huge, healing dose of something neuroscience calls “collective effervescence.” This word for a joyous crowd vibe is a powerful form of awe that has been found to be a deeply healing and unifying emotion. Awe-filled moments of unity have been shown to increase our sense of connection and humanity.

Collective Effervescence

This collective spirit of engagement and oneness spreads quickly and feels magical. We can infuse these joyous vibes in person at an event as well as by watching social media reels. Collective effervescence is a sociological phrase coined by Émile Durkheim in 1911 that describes an intensely engaging human experience at a gathering. He typically studied these experiences at religious rituals to understand the fervor and power of human gatherings. Over the past century, the term has expanded to a broader meaning and can apply to gatherings of people who are united for purpose or pleasure. Neuroscience research that has examined emotional states of awe has found that collective effervescence is a truly awe-inducing experience.

Researcher and author Dacher Keltner has studied the healing benefits of collective effervescence and shows how shared moments at events such as games, concerts, and celebrations spark bursts of awe that transform us. In his book, Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life, he declares, “How does awe transform us? By quieting the nagging, self-critical, overbearing, status-conscious voice of our self or ego, and empowering us to collaborate, to open our minds to wonders, and to see the deep patterns of life.”

Awe draws us out of overthinking, rumination, and social anxiety. According to neuroscience, awe deactivates the default mode network (DMN) of our brains that controls self-referential thinking and anticipating outcomes (predictive coding). A burst of awe brings us into the present moment and breaks us out of the grip of our thoughts. A wildly beautiful moment of collective effervescence shifts our focus from ourselves outwards to others around us.

Sitting with hundreds of fans and locals in a wave of joy at a restaurant in Boston on the eve of the big match, I felt the collective effervescence take hold, and I willingly disappeared into the vastness of the vibe. Awestruck, enchanted by the chanting, my sense of self shifted into a glorious sense of oneness with hundreds of souls. Time seemed to stop, and this feeling was indescribable. This present moment was all that mattered, and nothing was going to distract me from this breathtaking experience.

What the Awe Experience Scale Reveals

Research shows that we can validate and understand our moments of awe through a fascinating tool called the Awe Experience Scale. Psychologists (Yaden, Kaufman, Chirico, Keltner, and others) developed a scale to help us recognize our awe experiences by examining six factors that indicate we have lived through a real moment of awe.

Taking a bold next step to apply these six factors of awe experiences to the World Cup events, I would like to explore the impact of collective effervescence on the fans, locals, and other visitors around Boston.

In short, we could think of these six factors as the “wow” factors that brought awe to almost everyone watching the matches (at huge watch parties as well as at the stadium).

  1. The Perception of Vastness: One could look out over a sea of humanity and colorful flags from many visiting nations mixing in with locals. The vastness of the crowds spread throughout the parks, the streets, the Boston Common, playgrounds, on boats, on trains, on trolleys, duck boat tours, and buses (even school buses).
  2. Need for Accommodation: The experience was indescribable and overwhelming—and yet invigorating. It was not possible to comprehend the experience all at once as it was intensely profound. It was an experience to wonder about and ponder for days afterwards.
  3. Alterations in Time: Fully in the present moment, time seemed to stop, slow down, or stand still.
  4. Self-diminishment (or a sense of the small self): Amid the wide sea of humanity and international unity, people felt part of a much wider world around them. They felt small, in a good way, as they reached beyond their individual sense of self to feel the enormity of a universal force.
  5. Connectedness: The people in the crowds felt a sense of oneness, belonging, and connection with others. Singing, dancing, chanting, cheering, playing—all brought people together.
  6. Physical Sensations: Participants felt chills, goosebumps, gasps, and other sensations as they joined in the joy of the moment.

Given these six factors of awe, even one or two of these can validate that we have had a true experience of amazement, enchantment, astonishment—all part of this powerful emotion. And it opens our eyes.

Dacher Keltner tells us that awe is “the feeling of being in the presence of something vast that transcends your current understanding of the world.”

Considering Keltner’s definition of awe: Yes, the World Cup fans have transformed the people of Boston and other host cities. Yes, these events transcended our understanding of the world. These games have beckoned us to see one another in a new light—even people from Iraq, Norway, Morocco, Scotland, and many more.

I would like to offer that the awe of collective effervescence can happen whenever we join in a “group vibe” that connects us, unites us, and eases isolation and social anxiety. Thankfully, the fans of the FIFA World Cup have brought a much-needed spark of connection and community to many American host cities, showing the world that, indeed, Americans can be amazing people to hang out with.

Even if it's only in brief or fleeting moments, that collective sense of feeling alive makes an unforgettable difference to us. We can treasure these experiences as testaments of joy, hope, and the beauty of the human spirit. These wondrous moments restore our sense of belonging and can even heal an entire city—and maybe heal the troubled hearts of most Americans in these turbulent times.

item.title: How a "Change Sampler" Can Help You Reach Your Goals
item.description:
Motivation

How a "Change Sampler" Can Help You Reach Your Goals

Successful change comes in small doses, not all at once.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Change is hard, and trying to make several big changes all at once often fails spectacularly.
  • A better approach may be a "change sampler," which involves reasonable goals and is time-bounded.
  • It's important to start with an attitude of curiosity rather than do-or-die determination.
  • It helps to track our progress so we can fine-tune our plans as we go along.
Source: tumisu/pixabay

Perhaps you do it in January, on your birthday, when you’re finally fed up or have painted yourself into a corner. The resolution, the campaign, the “this time” declaration that you’re finally going to do what you haven’t been doing.

You probably know what happens next: You drop your gym membership a month after you started; you’re back to having that glass of wine or that bowl of pot “to help you relax” after a couple of weeks; you pay your bills or clean up your bedroom three weekends in a row, but then it’s over, all except for the kicking yourself.

Often, the problem is that you’ve taken too big a bite; your campaign is a white-knuckled, forced march through hell. If this rings true, I have a suggestion for you. Rather than diving into the water from the high dive platform, wade in with baby steps, the way you tested the waters when you were a kid. Challenge yourself to one week of change, doing what you haven’t been able to do successfully. Just one week—call it a change sampler.

The Benefits of a "Change Sampler"

  1. You get a taste of what it feels like. This helps you understand what’s too much, too little, and what’s just right.
  2. You’re still rewiring your brain, breaking habits and routines that keep you on autopilot. Just as the most important part of dealing with anxiety is learning to approach and gradually tolerate the feeling of anxiety, this baby-step pace lets you gradually tolerate change, and that is the ultimate goal.
  3. You adopt an attitude of curiosity and experimentation, stepping back, reducing pressure, observing, and making adjustments. The forced-march approach is myopic, with tunnel vision. You’re only able to see your feet rather than what lies ahead and the bigger landscape.

Ground Rules for Trying a "Change Sampler" in Your Own Life

  • It’s only for one week. After that, you can decide what’s next.
  • You set the pace. Whatever you're doing may not be every day, but a few days a week. Or not three hours, but one, or half, not all. The goal is to start with something realistic that has a chance of success.
  • Chart your experience. Like a scientist conducting an experiment, take notes; at the end of the day, assess what you did, how it felt, and lessons learned.
  • Tell others or not; it’s up to you. If telling others what you’re doing helps with support and accountability, tell them. If it’s going to just put more pressure on you, don’t.

Some suggestions:

  • Cut back on your strongest habits and vices—whether that's drinking too much, smoking too much, eating too much, watching porn, scrolling social media, etc.
  • Change your weekend, day off, or after-work routines.
  • Change what you wear.
  • Journal more, meditate more, exercise more.
  • Do what you’ve been procrastinating on: pay bills, file taxes, paint your deck.
  • Clean more or clean less.
  • Take a social risk: Go to a party you would generally avoid; speak up in a meeting where you normally wouldn't; call up an old friend; etc.
  • Re-engage in a hobby you’ve dropped: drawing, playing a musical instrument, knitting, birdwatching, etc.
  • Be more affectionate and/or complimentary toward your partner, your kids, or the people you work with or supervise.

How to Assess Your Progress After a Week of Small Changes

After one week of this, pause and take stock. How do you feel? What changes have you noticed in yourself, your attitude about yourself, your relationships, your view of your life?

What are the next steps? Do you want to do it again? Would it help to change the pace? Focus on something different? Go back to what you were doing before, maybe with a different attitude—or not?

Regardless of the answers, a change sampler is a win-win experience. You can’t do it wrong or badly—at least if you approach it with this stance of curiosity and experimentation. If you're ready, give it a try and see what happens. You might be surprised by what you discover.

item.title: Why We Want What We Want
item.description:
Decision-Making

Why We Want What We Want

What sticks, what sells, and what we pass on to our children.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Many of our strongest desires feel entirely personal until we discover they were planted by someone else.
  • Advertisers teach us how messages stick. Parents can use the same principles to teach wisdom.
  • Kids who practice discernment early are better prepared for a world designed to capture attention.

“I feel like Chicken Tonight… like Chicken Tonight.”

In a 1994 episode of "The Simpsons," the family gathers around a birthday cake, trying to sing together. Grandpa prompts Bart and Lisa to start a song. Lisa asks whether this family knows anything other than commercials. Apparently not. Instead of folk songs, camp songs, hymns, or family memories, what rises first is an advertising jingle for a chicken pasta sauce. They flap their arms like chickens and belt it out.

The joke works because it is the laugh of recognition. We've all been there: A group of people who cannot remember where they left their keys can somehow recite a marketing hook from 30 years ago. Commercial language has found a home inside our collective memory. Long before algorithmic feeds, advertisers understood that repeated language enters consciousness and stays there.

Advertisers have traded on this for a century, ever since the first radio jingle, a barbershop quartet singing “Have you tried Wheaties?” on Christmas Eve 1926. The Oscar Mayer bologna song, Meow Mix in ‘74, even that operatic J.G. Wentworth “877-CASH-NOW”: Rhythm and repetition embed themselves whether we want them to or not. Language fused with music sinks in and takes root. The earworm is not a bug. It’s the business model.

Do parents fully grasp the power of compressed repeated language in the home? Have counter-jingles been planted? Family sayings? Short poetic phrases about values, attention, judgment? Or have those lessons been delivered mostly through long explanations that are forgotten almost as quickly as they are spoken? What have we installed in them that will survive our expiration date?

The Grocery Store Is a Stage

The grocery store may be one of the first great stages where children encounter the constructed world. The lighting, shelf placement, and mascot faces do not feel theatrical because we have been performing inside them our entire lives. The family thinks it is shopping. It has entered an environment carefully engineered to influence behavior. Think Disneyland Lite with cheaper prices and better parking.

The grocery store may be one of the first places children encounter how the world is deliberately designed.
Source: Kleomenis Spyroglou / Unsplash

Kids are active participants in this environment. Products aimed at them are often placed near their sightline. Mega-companies compete for better placement because visibility becomes desire. The child is not simply asking for things. The store has often asked first.

Then comes the performance adults usually call a tantrum. The mascot is familiar. The bright colors were chosen. The commercial may already have rehearsed the desire at home. The shelf made the product reachable. The checkout line made refusal public.

The scene has been directed before the parent ever says no. The register area is the store’s closing argument. One last push in a negotiation that began several aisles earlier. Marketers call it “pester factor,” making children sound as though they arrive with a trick up their sleeve.

But Professor Emma Boyland’s May 2026 study points to a more heartbreaking reality: Parents experiencing food insecurity face the most frequent pestering, turning grocery shopping into profound distress. To an outside observer, the child looks greedy and manipulative. Viewed through the lens of scarcity, the same behavior looks very different. Sometimes the meltdown is an SOS. Imagine taking a child living in a shelter on a tour of homes in Architectural Digest. "Water, water, everywhere, nor any drop to drink." The kid having a tantrum may be the one most in need of relief. Maybe give the kids a break. They are easy prey. The grocery store is just the first classroom. The algorithm will be the next one, and it may know them better than we do.

Wanting vs. Liking

The vulnerability is biological. Psychologist Kent Berridge’s work suggests that wanting and liking are separate neurological tracks. Cues create intense forms of wanting before we ever reflect on whether we actually like the thing itself. We know not to go shopping hungry because hunger changes desire. The child wants the cereal. The adult thinks they need the latest energy drink on display. The child isn’t less sophisticated. Just more honest.

When I was a child, I wanted Popeye spinach. Not spinach. Popeye spinach, in a can. I had seen what it did to the sailor man. Power. My mother told me it did not work like that. She gave in because I suppose there are worse things than a child begging for spinach. Reality did its work. I ate it. No instant strength arrived. The cartoon promise failed. I wanted it, but I did not like it. The desire underneath did not disappear, however. A few years later, I started lifting weights.

I imagine the creators of Popeye understood something real about children: Fantasy can move behavior. Culture rarely gives children pure messages. Kids absorb inspiration, confusion, aspiration, contradiction, and commerce all tangled together. Discernment does not require perfect models. It requires learning how to sort, test, revise, and reconstruct meaning from imperfect ones. Children attach deep wishes to concrete objects. The spinach carried a wish for power. The object was easy to see. The wish was not.

Counter-Jingles

Madison Avenue knows that what sticks often wins. Your child’s memory is their long game. What else are you installing alongside it? Wisdom has to compete for mental shelf space. This doesn’t require matching their budget. A parent’s voice has something no marketing firm can buy: proximity and trust. But they are not enough on their own. The lesson has to be repeatable. It has to have enough rhythm and artfulness to survive.

This is where parental honesty matters. “Don’t ask for anything. We’re only getting what we came for.” Then the adult remembers something they need. Another item enters the cart. Then another. Children can survive disappointment. Contradiction is harder. Restraint becomes hypocrisy, and they notice.

What if the adult said something else? “I really want this. But it’s possible this big red sign is influencing me. Let’s take a picture of it and see if we still want it next time.” “I feel the pull, but is it real? Let’s wait and see how the want will feel." The pause is a lab test. The family aphorism becomes a shared tool for seeing the seams of the world. Short, memorable, repeatable. Coming from a parent, it carries a weight that a corporate jingle cannot mimic. Eventually, the child learns that the pause itself is the skill.

What They Can Carry

Kids often comprehend more than they can articulate. As a child, I wore a hat covered in peace signs, smiley faces, and an R. Crumb “Keep On Truckin’” button, the exact same one Tony Danza had tattooed on his arm to look cool. I knew the messages mattered. Peace, happiness, perseverance. Entire aspirations compressed into symbols small enough to wear on a hat.

Children are not ours to break. They are ours to shepherd. Talk with them. Guide them. But leave them something they can carry.

And if you suddenly feel like Chicken Tonight, by all means, flap your wings and sing it out. Just know how the song got there.

item.title: FIFA and a Ruling of Mistaken Identity
item.description:
Sport and Competition

FIFA and a Ruling of Mistaken Identity

Rules in sports and play spark both confusion and creativity.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Regulation and creativity constantly clash in sports.
  • Sports rule-making drives both innovation and more chances for rule-breaking and mischief.
  • Play-inspired, divergent thinking often leads to delight and discovery.
Jeff Daniels, a wry fellow pictured here at the Montclair Film Festival, performs as half of the Dumb and Dumber team.
Source: Image courtesy Montclair Film, via Wikimedia (May 5, 2018).

At risk of some reputational damage, I confess that one of my favorite comic scenes has “Dumb”—the Jeff Daniels character in the sequel Dumb and Dumber To—stumbling onto the stage of a TED Talk- like conference where he is taken for a world-renowned scientist slated to comment on the presentations.

On stage, a young genius describes how he has invented an injectable nanobot that seeks out and destroys cancer cells. The audience, revved up for revelation, gasps in astonishment and admiration.

“Interesting…” says Daniels’ goofy character. “But. Does it sing?” The question baffles the inventor. And the impostor explains that now “they’ve got a largemouth bass that you hang on the wall, and it sings “Take Me to the River.” “What I’m saying is,” he continues, sagely, “is that you’re this close, and there’s a drawing board that you should be getting back to. Next!” Mystified, the budding scientist says, “But it cures cancer…”

FIFA Refs and the Mistaken Identity Law

Mistaken identity takes hold of more memorable comic films, making life twisty and dangerous for main characters. Hitchcock’s North by Northwest is one good example; The Big Lebowski is another. But I couldn’t imagine that mistaken identity could have anything to do with World Cup soccer until the United States team faced off against Uruguay in the opening round.

This recent instance is mistaken identity of a peculiar kind. In that match, the FIFA referee cited the American captain for a tripping foul and levied a free kick. (A free kick results in a goal three times out of four, and so could well have decided the game.) But a video review rescinded the penalty, a first instance of a new technology applied to enforcing a newly promulgated rule.

The updated official “laws” of soccer (fútbol) had provided for a reversal in the case that the referee had “clearly penalised the wrong player of either team for the offence in question.” The rulebook noted: “The offence itself cannot be reviewed except in the context of mistaken identity.”

Some Rules Are Hard to Follow

If the context of “mistaken identity” itself seems unnecessarily inside and technical here (misleading, too, because nobody on the pitch was taken for somebody else), know that the obscurity is not an exception.

I once asked other parents of soccer daughters, our Buffalo Rockets, for help in explaining the off-side rule. That group included three lawyers, an administrative judge, and a dentist. They delivered five different impressions.

Looking for clarity and simplicity, I found instead that the text for Law 11, including commentary and exceptions to the off-side rule, ran to three full, single-spaced pages.

From Boundlessness to Consolidation

We don’t need to strain to find instances where informal games, those that kids first played and negotiated spontaneously on the lawn or in the street, became increasingly organized by and for adults, and sometimes rapidly. While it took centuries for golf to settle on its governance, and decades for American football to evolve into its modern form, other sports went from casual to codified in record time. Think of two: frisbee and pickleball.

Frisbee, with its origins in the counterculture—a favorite on college quadrangles in the 1970s and an improvised pick-up game if there's ever been one—has now garnered notice from the International Olympic Committee. “Ultimate Frisbee” even boasts rival governing committees. The rulebook for one of these specifies the size of the field, the equipment allowed, and the rhythm of the game. It features seven appendices.

Or more recently, consider pickleball. Once played in backyards with repurposed tennis racquets, pickleball has its own new gear and is reputed to be the fastest-growing sport worldwide. True to form, pickleball play has been codified. Operating within artificial restraints and restrictions has unearthed more bones of contention. These needed to be diagnosed and mended. The 2026 USA Official Pickleball Rulebook runs to 96 pages. Rules are rules.

This tendency toward systematizing also creates more occasion for infraction. Rulemaking, let it be said, also invites rule-breaking, as subversion and mischief reliably become part of the experience and parcel of the fun.

Playful Repurposing

Some innovations have been accidental. Two famous examples show how original purposes inadvertently diverged into classic toys. Silly Putty resulted from a failed attempt to create artificial rubber during World War II when Japanese conquest cut off supplies of natural rubber. (A clever marketer later saw in the substance the potential for a gooey plaything.) And Play-Doh, another perennial favorite, began as a tool to scrub soot from wallpaper. Players will now roll up a brilliant pink hot dog or a yellow dachshund long after coal ceased to heat houses.

Divergent Thinking and Innovation

So, when thinking diverges from the worn path, interesting things can happen—sometimes, for the better. Purposeful, play-inspired methods now consciously deploy divergent thinking to encourage innovation and invention that management theorists term “delight-driven.”

One of these approaches that means to encourage teams toward creative, original solutions goes by the acronym SCAMPER—Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, and Redirect (or Reverse). Why not mash up a music player that can store songs with a portable phone enabled to hook up to the internet? Hmmmm. Why not?

The most successful and innovative organizations leave themselves open to pursuing innovation by generating a generous store of ideas. Some pay off. For the lucky team or individual mind, divergence converges on workable, original solutions.

Divergence vs. Disruption

Of course, sometimes divergence disrupts. Consider the heap of products that invention left behind. The phonograph. Stick shifts. Film cameras. The atlas. Car keys. And who knows what next? Landlines? Internal combustion engines? Currency? Scalpels?

Or consider the wreckage of once serviceable but dead-end rational beliefs—astrology, heliocentrism, the geology of Noah’s Flood, phrenology, homeopathy, “scientific” racism, cold fusion, and so on.

But back to Dumb and Dumber and disruption. Rather than intellectually challenged, the disorderly duo are instead wildly mistaken, comically misinformed, tacky beyond salvation, and especially, badly behaved. There is, alas, a lot of that going around.

Mistaken for eminent scientists at a key TED-like presentation, of course they revert. Their catcalls, however infantile, compel a celebrated scientist to reconsider his conclusion. He admits, tearfully, that his cosmos-shaking claims about dark matter were data-thin and speculation-heavy. He needs to go back to the drawing board. Soaring paradigms fall when wobbly foundations erode.

Play and other creative endeavors will lurch between regulation and abandon, order and disorder, and conformity and creativity.

item.title: After Social Media’s Trial, Is AI Next?
item.description:
Education

After Social Media’s Trial, Is AI Next?

How AI could become the next mental health debate on college campuses.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Universities are rapidly integrating AI without long-term psychological data.
  • Social media lawsuits may influence future AI policy on college campuses.
  • Courts are beginning to examine how digital systems shape human behavior.
  • Undergrad students must navigate evolving AI’s ethical challenges in real time.

Recent social media lawsuits may ultimately shape the future of artificial intelligence (AI) on college campuses. As courts begin examining whether social media companies can be held responsible for the psychological effects of their platform design, universities and mental health professionals are watching closely. These cases are beginning to shift public conversation away from individual user behavior and toward the broader influence of digital systems engineered to shape the attention, engagement, and decision-making of our youth.

While current legal scrutiny is centered on platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube, professors already confirm that similar conversations are emerging around AI in higher education. AI tools are already becoming embedded into how college students learn, write, communicate, organize information, and process ideas. As universities rapidly integrate these systems into classrooms and campus life, the social media lawsuits unfolding today may offer an early preview of the ethical, psychological, and legal questions AI could face tomorrow.

The challenge is that universities are rapidly adopting AI technologies without fully understanding their long-term psychological impact on the generation growing up alongside them. This question inevitably leads to a crisis of responsibility. When corporations are financially driven to maximize engagement, the concept of self-regulation becomes a paradox. Furthermore, if the human brain, particularly the developing adolescent brain, struggles to disengage from systems designed to exploit its neurological reward pathways, it is no longer scientifically sound to place the burden of responsibility solely on the individual user. For the mental health professional, this shift marks a new era in clinical practice.

Why This Matters for AI

This urgency of addressing this issue stems from the reality that AI is now a permanent part of our daily routines. Like social media before it, AI is not a neutral force. These systems are built with specific goals and trained on data sets that optimize for certain behaviors, often in ways that are subtle or entirely invisible to the user. If we acknowledge that design can dictate behavior, we must ask where our ethical responsibility begins. AI systems today are already beginning to shape human decision-making, interpersonal communication, and deep emotional experiences.

Source: AI-generated by Dr. Jessica Kizorek via ChatGPT / OpenAI, 5-5-2026

Regulation remains fragmented, creating a significant amount of uncertainty. Policymakers are struggling to balance the drive for innovation with the psychological necessity of safeguards. In the academic environment, students are articulating a need for more than just technical proficiency. Otis Kopp, a professor at Florida International University (FIU), observes that the current regulatory shifts are a necessary reaction to the speed of innovation. "We are reaching a point where the speed of technological integration has outpaced our psychological drafting of safety protocols," Kopp notes. "Legislation is finally acknowledging that the cognitive load placed on students by these pervasive systems requires more than just individual willpower; it requires structural guardrails."

The Role of Higher Education

Universities now find themselves at the center of this transition. They are not merely teaching students how to use new tools; they are shaping the ethical identities of the people who will design and regulate them in the future. This is especially critical for those entering the mental health field. Future clinicians must understand the architecture of the digital systems that affect their patients' lives.

In the modern classroom, the psychological impact of digital environments is no longer theoretical. For the college professor, the evidence is present in every lecture hall through shortened attention spans, the pull of digital engagement, and the rise of anxiety about both using AI and being forced not to. What we once categorized as a simple behavioral issue among the youth is increasingly revealing itself to be present in the overwhelming majority of young adults.

Jessica Kizorek, a professor at Florida International University, suggests that the goal of modern education is to build the resilience and awareness necessary to navigate this uncertainty. "We are training students for a future we can’t fully predict," she explains. "The goal isn’t to have perfect answers. It’s to help them build the confidence and awareness to navigate uncertainty responsibly."

What Comes Next

While legal appeals will likely continue for years, the broader cultural direction is clear. This broader direction is beginning to come into focus. Society is starting to evaluate technology not only for what it can do, but for how it shapes the people who use it…and that shift is increasingly relevant for mental health professionals. Clinicians are seeing firsthand how digital environments influence attention, mood, and self-perception, often in ways patients struggle to articulate. What once felt like background noise in a patient’s life is now emerging as a central factor in how they think, feel, and relate to the world around them.

Source: AI-generated by Dr. Jessica Kizorek via ChatGPT / OpenAI, 5-5-2026

This dynamic is especially important in the context of college students, who occupy a unique and complex position. They are not only among the most active users of these platforms but also the next generation of mental health providers, physicians, and caregivers. They are learning how to diagnose, treat, and support others, all while navigating the same systems that may be shaping their own habits, attention, and emotional resilience.

Universities are uniquely positioned in this moment. They are not only teaching students how to use emerging technologies but also shaping how those students will design, question, and regulate them in the future. In many classrooms, students are encouraged to look beyond the interface and consider the human impact of the systems they engage with daily. This creates an opportunity to build not just technical skill but awareness, empathy, and ethical responsibility.

As these students move into professional roles, they will carry both perspectives with them: The lived experience of being influenced by these systems and the responsibility of caring for others who are as well. That dual awareness may ultimately become one of the most important tools in modern mental health care.

The future of this field will not be shaped solely by new treatments or technologies but by the people who understand how to navigate both—people who are willing to ask not just what is possible but what is healthy, sustainable, and human.

item.title: Why Algorithms Show Us What We Claim Not to Want
item.description:
Attention

Why Algorithms Show Us What We Claim Not to Want

Engagement follows behavior, not stated preferences.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • What we say we want from our feeds often conflicts with what captures our attention.
  • Engagement reflects actual behavior, not consciously stated preferences.
  • Negative and extreme content wins because human attention is threat-sensitive.
  • No algorithm can eliminate the tension because it reflects conflicting human goals, not a technical flaw.
Source: AI-generated; OpenAI/ChatGPT 5.2

Scroll X (née Twitter) for long enough and you’ll see a familiar complaint: Algorithms have ruined the feed. Users lament that posts no longer appear in a simple chronology and bristle at how often negative or disturbing news rises to the top. The usual solution quickly follows—calls for the algorithm to work differently, to show less of this and more of that (with “this” and “that” changing from post to post).

What often gets missed in these complaints is a simpler point: Algorithms' goal is to keep users engaged. They do that by showing content people reliably interact with. In that sense, they aren’t fundamentally different from other systems that adapt to human attention—whether that’s news outlets emphasizing negative stories because they draw clicks [1] or grocery stores optimizing what catches the eye on the shelf.

So why do algorithms, in particular, rub us the wrong way? I argue that our discomfort with them arises from a familiar mismatch: What we say we want from our information environment doesn’t always line up with how we actually behave when we’re immersed in it. Here's why that mismatch persists.

Are We All Just Hypocrites? It's Not So Simple

When people complain about what shows up in their feeds, it’s tempting to frame the issue as hypocrisy: You say you don’t want this, but you keep clicking on it. There’s a grain of truth there, but it’s also a lazy explanation. What’s really going on is less about dishonesty and more about conflict.

Humans, in general, are not especially good at introspecting about our own preferences—particularly when those preferences pull in different directions. In the abstract, many people genuinely want calmer, more uplifting, or more informative content. Those are the preferences we endorse when we’re asked to reflect, explain ourselves, or justify what a platform should be showing us. But once we’re immersed in a fast-moving stream of information, other forces kick in: curiosity, vigilance, outrage, novelty, and the low-level sense that this might matter.

Attention isn’t the same thing as endorsement. Interacting with a piece of content doesn’t necessarily mean we like it, agree with it, or want more of it in any broader sense. Often it just means the content was hard to ignore—especially when it taps into strong emotional or threat-related cues.

So the mismatch between what we say we want and what we actually engage with reflects the fact that our preferences aren’t stable, singular, or always accessible to conscious reflection. We can sincerely want one thing while repeatedly behaving in ways that pull us toward another. That tension is uncomfortable, but it’s also very human.

Why Negative and Extreme Content Keeps Winning

To understand why this mismatch shows up so reliably, it helps to revisit a familiar feature of human decision making: our sensitivity to potential threats and losses. From an evolutionary perspective, missing a genuine threat is often costlier than overreacting to a false alarm (Haselton & Nettle, 2006), so our attention systems are biased toward cues that signal risk, conflict, or uncertainty (Baumeister et al., 2001)—the kinds of posts people lament showing up in their feeds. Even when the stakes are low—as is typical on social media—those cues tug at the same underlying mechanisms.

This same dynamic can help explain why the media devotes so much attention to negative news. Content that reliably captures attention—because it’s alarming, controversial, or emotionally charged—doesn’t need to align with our long-term goals to win in the moment. It just needs to feel important right now—to activate values that prompt immediate action (Slovic, 1995), whether that’s a like, a comment, or a share.

Add in the fact that most people engage with feeds passively—which limits our ability to self-regulate—and a predictable pattern results: We gravitate toward content that activates strong cues, even as we insist that we’d prefer something else if given the choice.

None of this requires bad actors or malicious intent. It’s a natural consequence of how human attention works.

When There Is No “Should,” Systems Optimize for Engagement

This is where algorithms enter the picture—not necessarily as puppet masters, but simply as systems that deliver content based on our behavior.

Social media platforms don’t operate with a shared, widely accepted standard for which content should be shown to any given user. Outside of a strict chronological feed, deciding what should appear would require values-based curation [2]—agreement about what counts as appropriate, informative, or worthwhile. That kind of consensus simply doesn’t exist at scale.

In the absence of clear normative guidance, platforms tend to default to what they can measure. Engagement becomes the proxy for preference because it’s observable. Algorithms infer what matters to users by tracking what captures their attention and adjusting accordingly.

As such, a social media feed is a form of personalized choice architecture. Any system that structures which options are visible, salient, or easy to access influences decisions. Traditional choice architects—policymakers, designers, retailers—tend to rely on generalized assumptions about what people want or need. Algorithmic feeds flip that logic. Instead of nudging users based on abstract models of behavior, they continuously tailor the environment based on each individual’s past interactions.

The result is a personalized nudge toward what users reliably attend to in practice rather than toward what they say they want in principle. Over time, the feed becomes less a reflection of shared norms or editorial priorities and more a dynamic mirror of engagement patterns. It doesn’t ask which content would be best for you. It asks which content is most likely to keep you looking.

That’s not a moral judgment; it’s a design reality. And when put that way, the persistent frustration with algorithmic feeds looks less like a mystery and more like an unresolved tension between human attention and human aspiration.

Why No Algorithm Can Resolve the Conflict

The frustration people feel with algorithmic feeds is understandable. We want systems that reflect our values, not just our impulses. But when those values conflict with the ways our attention actually works, no amount of tweaking the feed will fully resolve the tension.

Algorithms don’t create that conflict; they expose it. They respond to what we do, not what we wish we did. And until we reckon with the gap between our aspirations and our behavior, the feeds we complain about will continue to feel both unsatisfying and uncomfortably familiar.

item.title: Can Shopping Increase Loneliness?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Can Shopping Increase Loneliness?

The surprising relationship between materialism and loneliness.

Posted June 22, 2026

Key points
  • Materialistic mindsets tend to increase loneliness.
  • Loneliness also increases materialism.
  • There is a time and place for treating yourself.

Be honest: Have you ever bought something to cure a bout of loneliness? It’s OK—I have, too! Social relationships and interactions with other people are among the most important determinants of day-to-day happiness. We intuitively understand that our moods are better when we are spending time with others, and a large body of scientific literature backs this finding. Despite this, a lot of people report being lonely. Approximately 20-33 percent of adults in the United States report being lonely on a weekly basis.1

Loneliness and Spending Money

I’m willing to bet you’ve heard the term retail therapy. When we’re in a funk (or lonely), we sometimes turn to shopping as an antidote to negative emotions. Buying something new can elicit excitement, joy, and comfort. Just as ibuprofen can cure pain temporarily for an injury, buying new things can curb loneliness in the short term as well.

But is this the whole story? Consumer researcher Rik Pieters investigated this question, which he called the "material trap." In other words, does being lonely increase materialism, which then further increases loneliness?

What the Research Says

To answer this interesting question, data were collected from more than 2,000 participants in the Netherlands five times over a six-year period (2005-2010). The study measured a variety of demographic variables such as gender, age, education, and income, along with the key variables of materialism and loneliness. Because measures were collected across time, the research was able to investigate whether loneliness reinforces materialism, whether materialism reinforces loneliness, or both.

The findings were clear: Loneliness increases materialism, which then perpetuates more loneliness. The loneliness-to-materialism pathway was the stronger one, although both were significant. Specific measures of loneliness illustrate how this unfolds psychologically. Loneliness increases materialism because lonely people agree more with concepts of possessions defining success (example statement: Some of the important achievements in life include acquiring material possessions) and that acquisition is a pursuit of happiness (example statement: I’d be happier if I could afford to buy more things).

For the materialism-to-loneliness pathway, higher agreement with acquisition centrality (example statement: I like a lot of luxury in my life) was the critical driver. When materialism is top of mind, people seem to become even more fixated on the acquisition and enjoyment of material purchases. Instead of calling up an old friend, they may go online to buy a new pair of shoes.

Explaining the Cycle and How to Break It

The relationship between loneliness and materialism is not one-way. Lonely people may turn toward possessions for comfort, status, or self-definition; over time, that material focus may further weaken social connection, creating a self-reinforcing loop.

Although buying new things is not a practical long-term replacement for social relationships, there is a time and place for treating yourself. Just as having an epic dessert or watching your favorite movie after a bad day can provide a much-needed pick-me-up, buying yourself something nice to boost your mood can be effective. Purchases are predictable, controllable, and immediately rewarding in ways that people may not be.

The danger is not enjoying nice things but, rather, asking our purchases to do the work of other people to make us feel worthy, loved, and included. Before making a purchase the next time you feel lonely, ask yourself, “What feeling am I hoping that this will give me?” If the answer is connection, status, or recognition, the unmet need may be relational rather than material. And if your gut tells you connection is what you really want, pause the purchase for 24 hours and use that same energy to get in touch with a friend to see if they are free for a meal or coffee soon.
